unit.name: Islam: Beliefs & Teachings
unit.subtitle: The six articles of faith, five roots of Usul ad-Din, and key beliefs in Sunni and Shi'a Islam

lessons.title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam
lessons.description: Sunni Six Articles of Faith and Shi'a Five Roots of Usul ad-Din compared side by side.
lessons.content_html:
Why Core Beliefs Matter

Islam is built on a set of core beliefs that shape every aspect of a Muslim’s life — from daily worship to moral decision-making. These beliefs are not identical across all Muslims. The two main branches of Islam, Sunni and Shi’a, share many fundamental ideas but organise and emphasise them differently. Understanding both frameworks is essential for the exam.

The split between Sunni and Shi’a originated after the Prophet Muhammad’s death in 632 CE. Most Muslims chose Abu Bakr as Caliph (successor), forming the Sunni tradition. A minority believed Muhammad had appointed his cousin and son-in-law Ali as the rightful leader, forming the Shi’a tradition. This disagreement over leadership led to different ways of expressing shared beliefs.

The Six Articles of Faith (Sunni Islam)

Sunni Muslims summarise their core beliefs in the Six Articles of Faith, collectively known as Iman. These six beliefs come from the Qur’an and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s teachings and example). Believing in all six is considered essential for a Sunni Muslim.

1. Tawhid — Oneness of Allah. There is only one God. Allah is eternal, absolute and has no partners or children. The sin of Shirk (associating anything with Allah) is the only unforgivable sin. Surah 112 declares: “He is Allah, the One.”

2. Malaikah — Angels. Allah created angels from divine light. They have no free will and carry out His commands perfectly. They deliver revelations to prophets and record every person’s deeds for the Day of Judgement.

3. Kutub — Holy Books. Allah revealed guidance through several scriptures, including the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Scrolls of Abraham and the Qur’an. Only the Qur’an is believed to remain uncorrupted — it is the direct, unchanged word of Allah.

4. Risalah — Prophethood. Allah chose prophets to deliver His message. Muhammad is the “Seal of the Prophets” — the final messenger. Surah 33:40 confirms this.

5. Akhirah — Day of Judgement and Afterlife. This life is a preparation for the next. Every person will be judged by Allah on the Day of Judgement. The righteous enter paradise (Jannah); the wicked face punishment in hell (Jahannam).

6. Al-Qadr — Predestination. Allah knows everything that has happened and will happen. Nothing occurs by chance. Surah 9:51 states: “Only what God has decreed will happen to us.”

Key Fact

The Six Articles of Faith are: (1) Tawhid, (2) Malaikah (angels), (3) Kutub (holy books), (4) Risalah (prophethood), (5) Akhirah (afterlife), and (6) Al-Qadr (predestination). Every Sunni Muslim must accept all six.

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi’a Islam)

Usul ad-Din means “foundations of the faith.” These five principles guide Shi’a belief, and from them flow the Ten Obligatory Acts that shape Shi’a practice.

1. Tawhid — Oneness of Allah. Identical to the Sunni belief. Allah is one, unique and beyond comparison.

2. Adalat — Divine Justice. Allah is perfectly just and never acts unfairly. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct.” Humans are accountable for their actions because Allah is fair in His judgement. This root is unique to Shi’a belief frameworks.

3. Nubuwwah — Prophethood. Allah sent prophets to guide humanity. Muhammad was the final prophet. This overlaps with the Sunni article of Risalah.

4. Imamate — Divinely Appointed Leadership. After Muhammad, twelve Imams from his family were chosen by Allah to lead the Muslim community. They are considered infallible. The twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, is believed to be in hiding and will return at the end of time. This belief has no equivalent in Sunni Islam.

5. Al-Ma’ad — Resurrection. On the Day of Judgement every person will be physically resurrected and judged by Allah on their deeds.

Key Fact

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din are: (1) Tawhid, (2) Adalat (justice), (3) Nubuwwah (prophethood), (4) Imamate (leadership), and (5) Al-Ma’ad (resurrection). The key differences from Sunni articles are the inclusion of Adalat and the Imamate.

Similarities and Differences

Both traditions share fundamental beliefs: the oneness of Allah (Tawhid), the authority of the Qur’an, the prophethood of Muhammad, and accountability on the Day of Judgement. They also carry out the same five key duties, though Shi’a Muslims list these inside the Ten Obligatory Acts rather than as the Five Pillars.

Leadership: Sunni Muslims accepted four Rightly Guided Caliphs. Shi’a Muslims believe only Ali and the twelve Imams had divine authority to lead.

Belief frameworks: Sunni Muslims follow six articles; Shi’a Muslims follow five roots. Shi’a belief uniquely includes Adalat (divine justice) and the Imamate. Sunni belief separately lists angels, holy books and predestination as individual articles.

Sources of authority: Sunni Muslims rely on the Qur’an, Sunnah and scholarly consensus. Shi’a Muslims also follow the teachings of the infallible Imams.

For the exam, you need to explain both frameworks clearly and identify what is shared and what is distinct. Remember that these differences stem from the original dispute over leadership — both groups worship the same God and follow the same Qur’an.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 4-mark “Explain Influence” question on a Beliefs paper might ask how belief in the Six Articles influences Sunni Muslims today. Structure your answer as: state the belief, explain what it means, then show how it affects daily life or worship. Always use Arabic terminology (Tawhid, Iman, Usul ad-Din) — this demonstrates subject-specific knowledge that earns marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sunni Muslims follow the Six Articles of Faith (Tawhid, angels, holy books, prophethood, afterlife, predestination). Shi’a Muslims follow the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Tawhid, Adalat, Nubuwwah, Imamate, Al-Ma’ad).
  • Both traditions share Tawhid, belief in Muhammad as the final prophet, and the Qur’an as the word of Allah. They differ mainly on leadership after Muhammad, with Shi’a Islam uniquely including Adalat and the Imamate.
  • The Sunni–Shi’a split began as a dispute over succession after Muhammad’s death in 632 CE but developed into genuinely different theological frameworks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in the Six Articles of Faith influences Sunni Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Belief in Tawhid means Sunni Muslims worship only Allah and avoid the sin of Shirk. This influences daily prayer, which is directed only to Allah, and means Muslims reject idol worship or placing anything alongside God.
• Belief in Akhirah (the afterlife) influences Muslims to live morally because they believe every action will be judged on the Day of Judgement. This motivates charitable acts, honesty and following the Sunnah.
• Belief in Al-Qadr (predestination) gives comfort during hardship because Muslims trust that everything happens according to Allah's plan. This influences their resilience and patience (sabr) in difficult times.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Usul ad-Din. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Adalat (Divine Justice): Shi'a Muslims believe Allah is perfectly just and never acts unfairly. Humans are accountable because Allah judges everyone fairly. This motivates Shi'a Muslims to pursue justice in their own lives.
• Imamate: Shi'a Muslims believe that twelve divinely appointed Imams from Muhammad's family were the rightful leaders after him. They are infallible and protect the true message of Islam. The twelfth Imam is believed to be in hiding.
• Source: Surah 16:90 — 'Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct' — supports the belief that Allah is just and expects justice from believers.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'There is no real difference between Sunni and Shi'a beliefs.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Both traditions share Tawhid — the absolute belief in one God. Surah 112 is central to both.
• Both accept Muhammad as the Seal of the Prophets (Surah 33:40) and follow the Qur'an as the uncorrupted word of Allah.
• Both believe in a Day of Judgement and accountability. Both carry out the same five key duties.

Arguments against:
• Shi'a belief includes Adalat (divine justice) as a separate root, emphasising Allah's fairness in a way the Sunni articles do not.
• The Imamate is a major theological difference — Shi'a Muslims believe in twelve infallible, divinely appointed Imams. Sunni Islam has no equivalent belief.
• Sunni belief lists angels and predestination as separate articles; Shi'a belief does not single them out as core roots.
• These differences lead to different sources of authority — Shi'a Muslims follow the teachings of the Imams alongside the Qur'an and Sunnah.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in Iman (the Six Articles) influences a Sunni Muslim's daily life.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Belief in Malaikah (angels) means Muslims are conscious that angels are recording every word and action. This influences them to behave morally at all times, not just when others are watching, because they know their deeds will be presented on the Day of Judgement.
• Belief in Kutub (holy books) means the Qur'an is treated as the supreme authority. Muslims read, memorise and follow its teachings daily. It guides decisions about prayer, diet, relationships and moral conduct.
[4 marks]

lessons.title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels
lessons.description: Tawhid, the qualities of Allah, His relationship with the world, and the nature and role of angels.
lessons.content_html:
Tawhid — The Oneness of God

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It means the absolute oneness of Allah — there is no God but Allah, and nothing can be compared to Him. Tawhid is the foundation of everything a Muslim believes and does. It is the first part of the Shahadah (declaration of faith): “There is no God but Allah.”

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the key Qur’anic text on Tawhid. It declares: “He is God the One, God the eternal. He begot no one nor was He begotten. No one is comparable to Him.” This short surah makes clear that Allah is unique, has always existed, was never created and cannot be compared to anything in creation.

Key Fact

Surah 112:1–4 is essential for the exam. It states that Allah is One, Eternal and Absolute, was not born and did not give birth, and nothing is comparable to Him. This surah is recited daily by Muslims and summarises the entire concept of Tawhid.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk — associating partners with Allah or giving God-like qualities to anything else. Shirk is considered the worst sin in Islam and the only sin Allah will not forgive. This is why Muslims do not create images of Allah or Muhammad, and why Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than depictions of God.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah has many qualities, described throughout the Qur’an. You need to know four key attributes:

Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful. He created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His ability. Qur'an 2:284 states: “To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth.… And Allah is over all things competent.”

Beneficence (Ar-Rahman): Allah is all-good and provides for His creation. Every surah of the Qur’an except one opens with: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Allah provides food, water, shelter and guidance for all people.

Mercy (Ar-Rahim): Allah is the Most Merciful. He forgives those who sincerely repent. Surah 39:53 says: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.” Muslims believe Allah’s mercy outweighs His wrath.

Fairness and Justice (Al-Adl): Allah treats all people fairly and never acts unjustly. Every person will be judged equally on the Day of Judgement. This quality is especially emphasised in Shi’a Islam as Adalat, one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din.

Adalat — justice in Shi’a Islam: While both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims agree that Allah is just, Shi’a Islam elevates this quality to one of its core beliefs. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct.” This means Allah will hold everyone accountable and will never punish the innocent.

Immanence and Transcendence

The spec asks about two contrasting ideas regarding Allah’s relationship with the world:

Transcendence means Allah is beyond and above creation. He exists outside of time, space and the physical world. Muslims emphasise that Allah is utterly different from anything humans can imagine — this is why Surah 112 says “No one is comparable to Him.” Allah cannot be fully understood by the human mind.

Immanence means Allah is present and involved in the world. Despite being beyond creation, Allah is closer to every person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16). He hears prayers, guides individuals and intervenes in the world. Muslims experience Allah’s immanence through prayer, the Qur’an and the natural world.

Key Fact

Muslims believe Allah is both transcendent (above and beyond creation) and immanent (close and involved in the world). These ideas are not contradictory — Allah is so powerful that He can be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16).

Angels (Malaikah)

Belief in angels is the second article of Sunni faith. Malaikah are beings created by Allah from divine light (Nur). Unlike humans, angels have no free will — they obey Allah’s commands without question. Surah 35:1 describes them as “messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings.”

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel. He delivered the Qur’an to the Prophet Muhammad over a period of 23 years, beginning in 610 CE during the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Without Jibril, Muhammad would not have received Allah’s revelation, and the Qur’an would not exist. Jibril also appeared to Ibrahim and Maryam (Mary), making him the chief messenger between Allah and humanity.

Mika’il (Michael) is the angel of mercy and provision. He is responsible for providing nourishment to human bodies and souls, and controls the natural world — rain, weather and harvest. Muslims believe Mika’il distributes Allah’s blessings throughout creation.

Angels perform several roles: they deliver revelations from Allah to prophets, they record every person’s good and bad deeds (the recording angels sit on each shoulder), they welcome the righteous into paradise, and they will be present at the Day of Judgement. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, and Azra’il (the Angel of Death) takes souls at the moment of death.

Belief in angels influences Muslims today because it reminds them that their actions are always being recorded. This encourages moral behaviour, honesty and mindfulness in daily life. If a Muslim is tempted to do wrong, the knowledge that an angel is recording the deed acts as a powerful deterrent.

Angels are central to Islam because they connect Allah to humanity. Without Jibril, the Qur’an would not have been revealed. Without the recording angels, there would be no account of human deeds for the Day of Judgement. Belief in Malaikah therefore reinforces belief in the Qur’an, prophethood and the afterlife — linking multiple articles of faith together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark “Explain with Sources” questions about Tawhid or the nature of God, always name and apply a specific Qur’anic source. The structure should be: state the belief clearly, explain what it means in practice, then quote a relevant source (e.g. Surah 112 for Tawhid, Surah 50:16 for immanence, Surah 39:53 for mercy). A well-applied source can earn up to 2 of the 6 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is the most fundamental belief in Islam, declared in Surah 112. The sin of Shirk — associating anything with Allah — is the only unforgivable sin.
  • Allah is described as omnipotent, beneficent, merciful, fair and just. He is both transcendent (beyond creation) and immanent (present in the world, closer than the jugular vein).
  • Angels (Malaikah) are created from light, have no free will, and carry out Allah’s commands. Jibril revealed the Qur’an to Muhammad; Mika’il provides sustenance and controls the natural world.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in Tawhid influences Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Tawhid means Muslims worship only Allah and reject all forms of Shirk. This influences daily life because Muslims do not create images of God, use only geometric patterns in mosques, and direct all prayer and devotion exclusively to Allah.
• Tawhid creates a sense of equality among Muslims — since only Allah is supreme, no human being is above another. This influences social relationships and community life, promoting fairness and humility.
• Tawhid shapes the Shahadah, which Muslims recite daily in prayer: 'There is no God but Allah.' This constant affirmation reinforces their commitment to monotheism.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about angels (Malaikah). Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks):
• Jibril is the most important angel because he revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years. Without Jibril, Muslims would not have received Allah's guidance. This makes Jibril the essential link between Allah and humanity.
• Recording angels sit on each person's shoulders and write down every good and bad deed. These records will be presented on the Day of Judgement. This belief influences Muslims to behave morally even when nobody is watching.
• Source: Surah 35:1 — describes angels as 'messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings' — showing they are powerful beings created to serve Allah.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in angels is the most important article of faith for Muslims.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• Without Jibril, the Qur'an would not have been revealed to Muhammad. The entire faith depends on this angelic role.
• Recording angels ensure accountability — they connect belief in God to the Day of Judgement.
• Israfil will announce the Day of Judgement; without angels, key events in Islamic eschatology could not occur.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is arguably more important because it is the foundation of all other beliefs. Without God, angels would not exist.
• The Shahadah begins with Tawhid, not with angels — this suggests Tawhid takes priority.
• Belief in the afterlife (Akhirah) could be seen as more important because it gives purpose to this life and motivates moral behaviour.
• All six articles work together — no single article is more important than the others.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in Allah's immanence and transcendence influences Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Belief in transcendence influences Muslims to show deep reverence in worship. Because Allah is beyond human understanding, Muslims remove their shoes in mosques, prostrate during prayer, and use respectful language when speaking about God.
• Belief in immanence gives Muslims confidence that Allah hears their prayers and is involved in their daily lives. Surah 50:16 says Allah is closer than the jugular vein, which encourages Muslims to turn to prayer in times of difficulty, trusting that Allah is present and responsive.
[4 marks]

lessons.title: Prophethood and the Holy Books
lessons.description: Prophethood (Risalah), the authority of the Qur'an and holy books, and the Shi'a Imamate.
lessons.content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but Jibril pressed him forcefully three times and commanded him to recite. As recorded in Sahih Bukhari (Hadith 3), the Prophet returned trembling, his heart beating severely. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering a 12-mark evaluation question about the importance of prophethood or the Qur’an, remember to consider both Sunni and Shi’a perspectives. Shi’a Muslims give additional authority to the Imams as interpreters of the Qur’an. Showing awareness of both traditions is how you weigh different points of view — essential for reaching the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Risalah (prophethood) means Allah sent prophets to guide humanity. Adam was the first, Ibrahim showed perfect submission, and Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets — the final messenger (Surah 33:40).
  • The Qur’an has supreme authority because it is the only holy book Muslims believe has never been corrupted. Previous books (Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Scrolls of Abraham) are respected but considered altered.
  • The Imamate is unique to Shi’a Islam. Twelve divinely appointed, infallible Imams succeeded Muhammad. The twelfth Imam is believed to be in hiding and will return at the end of time.

lessons.title: Predestination and Human Responsibility
lessons.description: Predestination, human freedom, the Day of Judgement, resurrection, heaven and hell in Islam.
lessons.content_html:
Al-Qadr — Predestination

Al-Qadr is the sixth article of Sunni faith. It means predestination — the belief that Allah already knows and has determined everything that will happen. Nothing occurs by accident or chance. Surah 9:51 states: “Only what God has decreed will happen to us. He is our Master.” This includes every event in a person’s life, from birth to death.

Muslims believe Allah has complete knowledge of the past, present and future. Before a child is born, an angel records four things about their life: their provision (livelihood), their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be happy or unhappy. This is written in the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh al-Mahfuz), which contains the record of all that has been and all that will be.

Key Fact

Al-Qadr does not mean humans are puppets. Muslims believe Allah knows in advance what choices a person will make, but the person still makes those choices freely. It is this freedom that makes humans accountable on the Day of Judgement.

Predestination and Human Freedom

One of the most complex issues in Islamic theology is how predestination relates to human freedom. If Allah has already decided everything, can humans truly be free? And if they are not free, how can they be held responsible for their actions on the Day of Judgement?

Most Muslims hold that both beliefs are true simultaneously. Allah’s knowledge is absolute — He knows what every person will do before they do it. But this foreknowledge does not force people to act in a particular way. Humans have genuine freedom of choice (ikhtiyar) and are responsible for their decisions. It is like a teacher who knows a student will fail an exam — the teacher’s knowledge did not cause the failure; the student’s lack of revision did.

Sunni view: Al-Qadr is one of the Six Articles of Faith. Sunni Muslims generally emphasise that everything happens according to Allah’s will. Even suffering and hardship are part of His plan. This belief gives comfort in difficult times — if something bad happens, a Muslim can trust it is part of Allah’s greater purpose, even if they cannot understand it.

Shi’a view: Shi’a Muslims place greater emphasis on Adalat (divine justice). They argue that Allah’s justice means He would not predetermine someone to sin and then punish them for it — that would be unjust. Shi’a theology therefore gives more weight to human free will, arguing that people genuinely choose their actions and are justly accountable for them.

Belief in Al-Qadr influences Muslims in practical ways. It encourages Sabr (patience) during hardship, because Muslims trust that suffering is part of Allah’s plan. It also encourages gratitude in good times, since all blessings come from Allah. However, it does not encourage passivity — Muslims are still expected to work hard, make good choices and strive to follow Allah’s guidance.

The Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din)

Muslims believe that this life is a test, and that every person will face judgement before Allah at the end of time. The Day of Judgement is described vividly in the Qur’an as a terrifying, earth-shaking event. Surah 99:1–2 states: “When the earth is shaken with its earthquake, and the earth discharges its burdens.”

On this day, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, and all living things will die. Then a second blast will resurrect every person who has ever lived. Each person will stand before Allah and their book of deeds — recorded by the angels throughout their life — will be opened. Those who receive their book in the right hand will enter paradise; those who receive it in the left hand will face punishment.

Surah 99:7–8 states: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.” This teaches that no action — however small — escapes Allah’s notice. Every good deed and every sin will be accounted for.

Surah 23:102–103 describes the scales of judgement: “Those whose good deeds weigh heavy will be successful, but those whose balance is light will have lost their souls for ever and will stay in Hell.” Good deeds are weighed against bad deeds, and the balance determines a person’s fate.

Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means life after death. Muslims believe the afterlife is eternal and that this earthly life is merely a temporary test. What a person does in this life determines their fate in the next. This belief underpins Muslim morality — every action carries consequences that extend beyond death.

Jannah (Paradise): The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of eternal peace, pleasure and closeness to Allah. Surah 47:15 describes rivers of water, milk, wine and honey, with fruits of every kind and forgiveness from Allah. Jannah has multiple levels, with the highest reserved for the most righteous. It is the ultimate reward for those who lived according to Allah’s will.

Jahannam (Hell): Jahannam is a place of torment and punishment for those who rejected Allah or lived sinfully without repentance. The Qur’an describes fire, boiling water and suffering. Surah 4:56 describes how the skin of those in hell will be replaced so they continue to feel the punishment. Most Muslims believe Jahannam can be temporary for sinful Muslims — Allah may forgive them and eventually admit them to paradise — but it is eternal for those who committed Shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah means Muslims see this life as a preparation for eternity. Every deed is recorded and will be judged. This motivates Muslims to pray, give charity, avoid sin and follow the Qur’an and Sunnah — because the stakes are not just for this life but for the life to come.

Human Responsibility and Accountability

The concepts of predestination, judgement and the afterlife work together to create a strong framework of personal accountability. Muslims believe every person is responsible for their own actions. No one can carry another’s sins (Surah 17:15). On the Day of Judgement, there are no excuses — the angels’ records are complete and Allah’s judgement is perfect.

This accountability influences how Muslims live. It encourages honesty, generosity, compassion and obedience to Allah. It discourages dishonesty, cruelty and arrogance, because Muslims know that even the smallest action — an “atom’s weight” — will be seen and judged. The belief in resurrection means there is no escape from this accountability, even in death.

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters Barzakh — a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement. In the grave, two angels (Munkar and Nakir) question the deceased about their faith: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?” A righteous person will answer correctly and experience comfort; a sinful person will struggle and experience suffering. This period lasts until the Day of Resurrection.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark evaluation question may present a statement like “Belief in the afterlife is the most important belief in Islam.” To reach the top band (10–12 marks), you must argue both sides with reasoned chains of logic. Use Qur’anic references (Surah 99:7–8 on the atom’s weight of deeds, Surah 9:51 on predestination) and explain how beliefs influence Muslim behaviour. Always reach a personal conclusion supported by evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Al-Qadr (predestination) means Allah knows everything in advance, but humans still have free will and are accountable for their choices. Shi’a Muslims emphasise Adalat (justice) to explain why free will is genuine.
  • On the Day of Judgement, every person will be resurrected and judged by Allah. Their book of deeds will determine whether they enter Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell).
  • Akhirah (life after death) is central to Muslim morality. This life is seen as a test, and every action — no matter how small — carries eternal consequences.

practice_questions.marks:

Arguments supporting:
• Akhirah gives purpose to this life — without belief in the afterlife, there would be less motivation to follow Allah's commands. This life is a test for the next.
• Surah 99:7–8 teaches that every deed, no matter how small, will be accounted for. This underpins all Muslim morality and worship.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is the most fundamental belief — it is the first part of the Shahadah and the basis of all other beliefs. Without God, there would be no afterlife.
• Belief in the Qur'an and prophethood could be seen as more important because they provide the guidance Muslims need to pass the test of this life.

lessons.title: Akhirah: Life After Death
lessons.description: Muslim beliefs about Barzakh, the Day of Judgement, paradise (Jannah) and hell (Jahannam).
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Muslims Believe in Life After Death?

For Muslims, death is not the end. It marks the beginning of a new stage of existence called Akhirah. This belief shapes how Muslims live every day, because they understand that their actions on Earth will be judged by Allah.

Muslims believe in Akhirah for several important reasons. The Qur’an teaches it directly, and since Muslims believe the Qur’an is the word of Allah, its teachings must be true. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) also taught about life after death. Akhirah is one of the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam and connects to Al-Ma’ad (resurrection), one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi’a Islam. Muslims also believe that life is a test from Allah, so there must be a time of reward and punishment to give that test meaning.

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah is one of the Six Articles of Faith for Sunni Muslims and connects to Al-Ma’ad (resurrection) in the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din for Shi’a Muslims. Both branches agree that all people will face judgement after death.

Barzakh — The Waiting Stage

When a Muslim dies, they enter a stage called Barzakh. This Arabic word means “barrier” — once a person crosses into Barzakh, they cannot return to earthly life. The soul remains conscious in the grave during this period.

Muslims believe that Allah sends two angels to question the dead person about their faith. Those who answer correctly will experience comfort and peace while they wait. Those who deny Allah will face punishment in the grave. The person remains in Barzakh until the Day of Judgement arrives.

Throughout a Muslim’s life, two angels sit on their shoulders recording every action. Raqib sits on the right shoulder and records good deeds, while Atid sits on the left and records bad deeds. These records form the “book of deeds” that will be presented on the Day of Judgement. As the Qur’an states: “The record of their deeds will be laid open and you will see the guilty, dismayed at what they contain” (Qur’an 18:49).

The Day of Judgement

Muslims believe that a day will come when Allah’s purpose for the universe has been fulfilled. The angel Israfil will blow a trumpet to announce the end of the world. The present world will be destroyed and then transformed into a new world. A second trumpet blast will signal the resurrection — every person who has ever lived will be raised from the dead with a new body to stand before Allah.

Allah will then judge each person based on their book of deeds. The Qur’an teaches that if a person receives their book in their right hand, they will enter paradise. If they receive it in their left hand, they will be sent to hell. This judgement is considered fair because Allah gave humans free will, making them responsible and accountable for their choices.

Key Fact

The Shi’a believe in Yawm al-Qiyamah (the Day of Judgement) as part of Al-Ma’ad. They teach that every Muslim and non-Muslim will be physically resurrected, judged by Allah, and asked to account for every word and action of their lives on Earth.

Jannah — Paradise

Jannah is described in the Qur’an as a beautiful, eternal garden — the final home for the faithful and righteous. The Qur’an promises: “And those who believe and do good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise, they dwell therein forever” (Qur’an 2:82).

According to Islamic teaching, Jannah has seven levels. Those with the greatest reward will reach the highest levels. People will be asked to recite from the Qur’an, and the more they can recite, the higher they go. In Jannah, families are reunited, no one grows old or becomes ill, and every wish is fulfilled. There are rivers, gardens, beautiful weather, and abundant food.

Muslims believe they will arrive at Jannah over the As-Sirat Bridge. The Qur’an describes Allah saying: “Enter among my servants! Enter My Paradise” (Qur’an 89:29–30). There are believed to be eight gates, each representing a good action such as giving to charity or completing Hajj. A person will be called to the gate that matches their greatest good deed. Two angels welcome people, saying “Peace be upon you — enter here and live within.”

Jahannam — Hell

Jahannam is described as a place of fire and terrible torment. The Qur’an warns: “They will dwell amid scorching wind and scalding water in the shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor refreshing” (Qur’an 56:42–44). It is the punishment for those who reject Allah and commit evil.

There are seven levels of Jahannam, with different punishments for different sins. The most serious sin is shirk (worshipping anything other than Allah), which is the only sin Allah will not forgive. However, for sinful believers, Jahannam can serve as a place of purification. When Allah chooses, He may move these believers on to Jannah.

The Qur’an and Hadith give several reasons why a person may be sent to Jahannam. These include living a wicked life full of evil, rejecting the teachings of the Qur’an, refusing to take responsibility for one’s sins by blaming others, and committing shirk. Some Muslims believe that polytheists will go to hell permanently, but that some non-Muslim monotheists may still be able to enter Jannah.

How Belief in Akhirah Influences Muslim Life

Belief in the afterlife has a powerful effect on how Muslims live. Because life on Earth is seen as a test from Allah, Muslims strive to do well in order to be rewarded in Akhirah. This belief encourages them to think carefully about their actions, behaviour, and choices every single day.

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah encourages human responsibility and accountability. It urges Muslims to avoid sin, seek forgiveness when they do wrong, perform sacred duties such as reading the Qur’an and following Shari’ah law, and treat every action as an act of worship (ibadah) to Allah.

Muslims are aware that angels are constantly watching and recording their deeds. This makes them more God-conscious (taqwa) in their daily lives. Belief in Akhirah also gives Muslims a sense of justice — the good will be rewarded and the wicked will be punished — and provides purpose and meaning to their lives on Earth.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on Akhirah, always distinguish between the different stages: Barzakh (waiting), the Day of Judgement (resurrection and weighing of deeds), and the final destinations of Jannah and Jahannam. For 6-mark questions, remember to include a specific Qur’an reference and explain how it connects to the belief. For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider arguments both for and against the importance of belief in life after death, and always include religious teachings to support your points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Akhirah is the Muslim belief in life after death, which includes Barzakh (the waiting stage), the Day of Judgement, and the eternal destinations of Jannah (paradise) and Jahannam (hell).
  • The angel Israfil will blow a trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, when all people will be resurrected and judged by Allah based on their recorded deeds.
  • Belief in Akhirah shapes Muslim daily life by encouraging responsibility, accountability, and the avoidance of sin, as every action is seen as preparation for judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the name for the waiting stage between death and the Day of Judgement in Islam?
(A) Jannah
(B) Barzakh
(C) Jahannam
(D) Shirk
practice_questions.marks: B — Barzakh [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two Muslim beliefs about Jahannam (hell).
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for giving two correct beliefs, such as:
• It is a place of fire and great torment
• It has seven levels with different punishments
• It is the punishment for those who reject Allah and do evil
• Shirk (idolatry) is the only unforgivable sin
• For sinful believers it can be a place of purification before moving to Jannah
• It is described as an eternal physical place
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief about divine judgement influences Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Muslims believe that on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din), every person’s deeds will be weighed. This influences Muslims to try to accumulate good deeds — praying, giving to charity (Zakat and Sadaqah), fasting, and helping others — because they believe the balance of good versus bad deeds will determine their fate in the afterlife.
• Belief in Jahannam (hell) influences Muslims to avoid haram (forbidden) actions such as drinking alcohol, gambling, and dishonesty. The fear of punishment acts as a deterrent, while the hope of Jannah (paradise) acts as a motivation to live righteously.
• The belief that Allah is also merciful (Ar-Rahman) influences Muslims to sincerely repent (tawbah) when they do wrong, because they believe Allah forgives those who genuinely turn back to him.
[4 marks — two developed points needed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about the Day of Judgement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Belief 1 (2 marks): Muslims believe that on the Day of Judgement, every person who has ever lived will be resurrected from the dead and given a new body. Allah will judge each person based on their recorded deeds.

Belief 2 (2 marks): Muslims believe that the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet to announce the end of the present world and the beginning of judgement. All people will then stand before Allah to account for their actions.

Source of authority (2 marks): The Qur’an states: ‘The record of their deeds will be laid open and you will see the guilty, dismayed at what they contain’ (Qur’an 18:49), which teaches that every deed, small or large, will be accounted for.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Muslim idea of paradise is just wishful thinking.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• There is no physical evidence that paradise exists — descriptions of rivers, gardens, and eternal youth could be human imagination
• The detailed descriptions of Jannah (beautiful gardens, abundant food, no ageing) seem too perfect and may reflect human desires rather than reality
• Non-religious people may argue that belief in an afterlife is a coping mechanism for the fear of death
• Different religions describe different afterlives, suggesting they are cultural constructs
Arguments against:
• Muslims believe the Qur’an is the word of Allah, so its descriptions of Jannah must be true: ‘Those who believe and do good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise, they dwell therein forever’ (Qur’an 2:82)
• The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) taught about Jannah, and as the final prophet his teachings carry divine authority
• Belief in Jannah gives Muslims a moral framework — it encourages good behaviour and accountability, which has real practical effects
• Akhirah is one of the Six Articles of Faith / Five Roots — it is a fundamental belief supported by centuries of Islamic scholarship
• The existence of Jannah reflects Allah’s justice and mercy, which are core attributes of God
Top band (10-12): Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different viewpoints. Logical reasoning supported by knowledge of relevant evidence. References to religion applied to the issue.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration of different viewpoints with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view, or recognition of different viewpoints with reasons.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s) stated.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief about life after death influences Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Way 1 (2 marks): Muslims believe that life on Earth is a test from Allah, so belief in Akhirah motivates them to live according to Islamic teachings. They will try to perform sacred duties such as prayer (salah), reading the Qur’an, and following Shari’ah law in order to be rewarded in the afterlife.

Way 2 (2 marks): Because Muslims believe that angels are recording their every deed, belief in the afterlife makes them more aware of their thoughts, actions, and behaviour. They will think carefully about their choices, seek forgiveness (tawbah) when they do wrong, and treat every action as an act of worship (ibadah) to Allah.
[4 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The Muslim belief in life after death, beginning at the moment a person dies.
A barrier or waiting stage between death and the Day of Judgement, where the soul remains conscious in the grave.
The angel who will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement and the destruction of the present world.
Paradise in Islam, described as an eternal garden of peace and reward for the faithful and righteous.
Hell in Islam, a place of fire and torment for those who reject Allah and do evil.
The sin of associating partners with Allah or worshipping anything other than Allah — the only sin Allah will not forgive.
